blocks.text: An agent that reacts one tool call at a time works fine for a single ask, but it stalls on anything bigger.
Agent planning means breaking a large goal into a sequence of smaller steps before any tool gets called, then working through that sequence one step at a time.
MCP makes this easier because an agent can look at what tools, resources, and prompts a server actually offers before it commits to a plan.
1. Why Agents Need a Plan

blocks.alt: An agent queries available tools, drafts a plan, executes steps, and re-plans if needed

blocks.text: Without a plan, an agent decides its next single action based only on the current prompt and whatever it just saw.
That works for a one step ask, but a goal like "prepare a release report" actually hides several smaller jobs, pulling commits, running tests, summarizing failures, and formatting output.
Planning forces the agent to name those smaller jobs up front, so it does not wander or repeat work it already did.

items: Fewer wasted tool calls, since the agent knows what it needs before it starts
Missing information gets caught early, before any real work has happened
The user gets a preview of what the agent intends to do
A failure later on is easier to isolate to one specific step

blocks.text: Think of it like planning a road trip, you decide the stops before you leave the driveway, instead of picking each turn as you go.
A plan also gives a human reviewer something concrete to look at before any action actually happens.
That upfront visibility matters even more once a Human in the Loop check gets added to a risky step.
2. Breaking a Goal into Steps

blocks.alt: One big goal breaks down into smaller ordered steps

blocks.text: The first job of a planner is decomposition, splitting one large ask into an ordered list of smaller, concrete steps.
Each step should be small enough that a single tool call, or a short handful of them, can finish it.
A useful test: if you cannot say whether a step succeeded or failed on its own, that step is still too big.
Decomposition does not need to be perfect on the first pass, a rough split is enough to start discovery.
3. Discovery Before Deciding
A planner that guesses which tools exist is fragile, since every MCP server can expose a different set of tools, resources, and prompts.
Before locking in a plan, a well built agent calls tools/list, resources/list, and prompts/list to see what is actually available right now.
That discovery step turns planning from a guess into a decision grounded in what the server can really do today.

blocks.title: Discovery is cheap
blocks.content: Listing tools, resources, and prompts is a lightweight read only call, so there is little cost to checking before every single plan.

blocks.text: Re-running discovery on every single plan also protects against a server that changed its tool set since the last connection.
4. Querying tools/list to Inform a Plan

blocks.alt: A tools list query informs which steps a plan can actually include

blocks.text: Here is an agent calling discovery first, then only building steps around tools that actually exist on the connected server.
Any step that references a tool the server does not actually have gets flagged as blocked before the agent wastes a single call on it.
5. Resources and Prompts as Planning Inputs
Tools are not the only planning input, resources tell the agent what data already exists that it could read instead of fetching it again.
Prompts published by a server can hand the agent a ready made template for a sub task, which changes what the plan even needs to include.
A planner that only looks at tools and ignores resources and prompts ends up reinventing steps the server already offers.

6. From Discovery to a Draft Plan
Once discovery finishes, the agent matches each sub task from decomposition against the tools and resources it just found.
Steps with no matching tool get flagged right away, before the agent has spent any real execution time on them.
The output of this stage is a draft plan, an ordered list of steps, each one tagged with the tool or resource it intends to use.
A draft plan is still just a proposal, nothing has actually run yet at this point.
7. Executing the Plan Step by Step

blocks.alt: A plan executes one step after another toward the goal

blocks.text: Execution walks the draft plan one step at a time, running the tool call for the current step and recording what comes back.
The agent checks the result against what the step expected before it moves on, rather than blindly advancing to the next line.
This check is what separates planning from a script, a script just runs top to bottom, a planning agent verifies as it goes.
8. When a Step Fails

blocks.alt: A failed step interrupts the plan before it can continue

blocks.text: A step can fail outright with an error from the tool, or it can fail quietly, returning a result that does not match what the plan expected.
Treating both as failures matters, because a wrong answer that looks like success is the more dangerous case to miss.

items: The tool call itself returns an error
The result is empty when the step expected real data
A returned value falls outside a sane or expected range
The next step in the plan cannot actually use the output it just got

blocks.text: 9. Re-planning After a Failure

blocks.alt: A failure leads to a revised plan rather than repeating the same steps

blocks.text: Re-planning means the agent revises the remaining steps in light of what just happened, instead of pretending the plan is still correct.
A good re-plan usually touches only the steps after the failure point, it does not throw away work that already succeeded.
10. Fixed Upfront Plans vs Adaptive Plans

blocks.alt: A fixed upfront plan is compared against an adaptive plan

blocks.text: A fixed plan is written once, before any tool runs, and the agent follows it in order no matter what results come back.
An adaptive plan treats each result as new information, and is willing to insert, remove, or reorder the steps that remain.
Fixed plans are simpler and easier to audit, adaptive plans handle surprises but cost more reasoning at every step.
Neither approach is universally correct, the right choice depends on how predictable the task actually is.

blocks.title: Pick fixed when the environment is stable
blocks.content: If tool results are reliable and the task is well understood, a fixed plan is cheaper to run and easier to review after the fact.

blocks.text: Most production agents actually use a mix, a fixed skeleton of major phases with adaptive re-planning inside each phase.
11. Planning and Long Running Tasks
A plan that spans hours or days needs its progress saved somewhere durable, not just held in memory.
The Long Running Sessions and Long Running Agents lessons cover exactly this kind of checkpointing in more depth.
A saved plan with a marked current step is what makes resuming after an interruption possible at all.
12. Choosing How Much to Re-plan
Not every failure needs a full restart, sometimes a single step can be retried with different arguments and the rest of the plan still holds.
A bigger surprise, like discovering a tool no longer exists, may mean the whole remaining plan needs to be rebuilt from scratch.
Good agents scope the re-plan to match the size of the surprise, small mismatch, small patch, structural surprise, full rebuild.
13. Worked Example
Goal: summarize the failed CI runs from this week and post the summary to the team channel.
The agent first calls tools/list and resources/list, and finds ci_runs, format_summary, and post_message, plus a resource holding the current channel roster.

items: Draft plan built: fetch ci_runs for the week, filter to failed runs, format_summary on the filtered set, post_message with the summary
Step one runs fine and returns twelve failed runs
Step three, format_summary, returns an empty string because the filter step actually passed zero rows through by mistake
The agent treats the empty output as a failed step, not a success, and re-plans
The re-plan adds a corrected filter step, reruns format_summary, then continues to post_message as originally planned

blocks.text: Only the broken middle step gets replaced, the successful fetch and the final post step stay exactly as they were.
The whole recovery took one extra tool call, not a full restart of the plan.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Skipping discovery and hard coding tool names, which breaks the moment a server changes its tool set
Treating any non error response as success, even when the content is empty or clearly wrong
Re-planning the entire task from scratch after every small failure, which wastes work that already succeeded
Writing a plan so vague that no single step has a clear pass or fail check
Never re-planning at all, so the agent keeps forcing a broken plan forward until it runs out of steps

blocks.text: 15. Practice
Take a multi step goal you already automate, like generating a weekly report, and write out its decomposition as a numbered list of steps.
For each step, write down what a passing result looks like and what a failing result looks like, before you write any tool calling code.
Then simulate one step failing on purpose and sketch what a minimal re-plan would change, versus what it would leave alone.
Finally, note which steps in your plan would benefit from a human approval before running.
16. Key Takeaway
Planning turns a vague goal into a checkable sequence of steps, and MCP discovery keeps that sequence grounded in what the server can actually do right now.
A plan that can notice a bad result and re-plan around it will always beat a fixed script that marches forward no matter what comes back.
Good discovery, a checkable plan, and a willingness to re-plan are the three habits that separate a reliable agent from a fragile one.
